The Menomonee Valley's Quiet Rezoning: Who Benefits When the City Plays Landlord?

A handful of developers got early access to city-held parcels along the Menomonee River corridor. We obtained the emails, the meeting notes, and the maps.

Marcus Trzeciak June 17, 2026  ·  14 min read

Illustration: The Menomonee Valley industrial corridor, looking west. The six parcels at issue are located between the Menomonee River Parkway and North 35th Street.

The emails arrived on a Tuesday in February, twelve days before the City of Milwaukee announced a public comment period on a proposed rezoning of six parcels in the Menomonee Valley corridor. But the two developers who would eventually submit the winning bids had already been briefed — privately, in a conference room at City Hall, over coffee provided by the Department of City Development.

The Ledger Room obtained those emails through an open records request filed in April. What they reveal is a process that, while not illegal under current city rules, raises serious questions about who has access to Milwaukee's land disposition process — and who doesn't.

"We were told the process was open. We found out later that the conversation had already happened."

— Karen Osei, executive director, Riverwest Community Development Corporation

The six parcels in question — totaling roughly 4.2 acres along the Menomonee River between North 31st and North 38th Streets — have been city-owned since 2011, when they were seized for unpaid taxes during the foreclosure crisis. Since then, they've sat mostly empty, used occasionally for illegal dumping and, during summer months, as informal parking for nearby businesses.

The Meeting That Wasn't on the Calendar

According to city records, a meeting between senior staff from the Department of City Development and representatives from Meridian Ridge Partners and Great Lakes Real Estate Group took place on February 7th, 2026. The meeting does not appear on any public calendar and was not disclosed in the department's weekly activity log, which is posted online.

Commissioner Diane Kowalczyk, who leads the Department of City Development, told The Ledger Room in an email that the February meeting was a "standard pre-submission conversation" of the type the department holds with "any interested party who requests a meeting." She did not respond to a follow-up question asking whether community organizations had been offered the same opportunity before the public comment period opened.

The department's own records suggest otherwise. Of the eleven entities that eventually submitted letters of interest during the official comment period, nine did so within the final three days of the window — suggesting that most organizations learned about the opportunity through word of mouth or press coverage, not early outreach from the city.

What the Developers Are Proposing

Meridian Ridge Partners, based in Brookfield, is proposing a mixed-use development on three of the six parcels: 74 market-rate apartments, approximately 8,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and a surface parking lot. The firm's principals have donated a combined $28,500 to Mayor Sandra Pruitt's campaign committee over the past four years.

Great Lakes Real Estate Group, based in Chicago with a Milwaukee satellite office, is proposing light industrial space on the remaining three parcels — specifically, "last-mile logistics" warehousing, a category that has faced significant community opposition in other Milwaukee neighborhoods due to its truck traffic and job quality concerns.

Neither proposal includes affordable housing. Neither proposal has been evaluated yet by the city's Planning Commission, though sources within city government tell The Ledger Room that an evaluation is expected before the end of the month.

Alderman Raymond Cortez, whose district includes the parcels, said he was "not informed of the February meeting" and learned of its existence when The Ledger Room contacted his office. He declined to characterize the meeting as improper but said he had "concerns about the process" that he intended to raise at the next council session.

The Community That Wasn't Consulted

Three blocks from the northernmost parcel, the Menomonee Valley Community Center has operated for twenty-two years. Its executive director, Tomás Villanueva, has been attending City Hall meetings about the Valley's future for nearly as long.

Villanueva submitted a letter of interest during the official comment period, on behalf of a coalition that includes the Community Center, two neighborhood associations, and a local CDFI. Their proposal: a community-owned land trust that would develop affordable live-work studios for artists and tradespeople on two of the six parcels, with the remaining land dedicated to a riverfront park.

"We put together a real proposal," Villanueva said. "We had financing commitments. We had a timeline. We had letters of support from seventeen neighborhood businesses. And we found out about the process through an article in the Journal Sentinel, twelve days after two other developers had already been walked through the city's expectations."

The community coalition's proposal has not been publicly ranked or evaluated. When The Ledger Room asked Commissioner Kowalczyk about its status, her office responded that "all submissions are under review."

The six parcels will be taken up by the full Common Council no earlier than August, according to a spokesperson for Council President Tamara Hines. Between now and then, the city's process will remain, in its own words, "under review."

Marcus Trzeciak covers city government and housing for The Ledger Room. He can be reached at marcus@theledgerroom.com.
